item.title: A critical look at self-distillation for reasoning
item.dc:creator: Jason Ken Adhinarta
Raina Wu
Zhang-Wei Hong
item.description:
This blog post summarizes our paper which will appear at the Transitioning from Pre-Training to Post-Training workshop at NeurIPS 2026. This is joint work with Ashutosh Sharma, Avinash Balakrishnan, and Rameswar Panda at the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab; along with Polina Golland and Yoon Kim at MIT CSAIL.

This post focuses on the main results; the paper covers detailed ablations and results across Qwen3 (1.7B–14B) and Olmo-3-7B-Instruct along with our experimental setup; we also provide code to reproduce our results.

arXiv Code

There has been a surge of interest in the self-distillation paradigm.

NoteWhat is self-distillation?

In typical policy gradient reinforcement learning (e.g., GRPO), a model is trained to increase its expected reward, through gradient ascent on . This provides coarse learning signals at the level of entire trajectories , which might require a large number of samples to learn effectively.

But we know that LLMs generate better solutions when given additional context. Namely, if we tell the model that the last time it tried to solve a task, it triggered ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'numpy', it probably won’t make the same mistake. So, why not train the model to behave as if it had access to this additional context?

In self-distillation, this additional context or privileged information can take many forms: reference solutions to math problems, code execution feedback, etc. In practice, in self-distillation we minimize the “difference” between the model’s behavior with and without privileged information along trajectories sampled without privileged information. Formally, we write: where is the stop-gradient operator, and is the privileged information, and is a choice of information divergence. With , looks a lot like .

However, several recent works have questioned the effectiveness of self-distillation. Self-distillation papers report impressive performance gains which are often hard to replicate. To study why, we carefully reproduce two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), and study the assumptions underlying self-distillation as presented in Shenfeld et al. We discover the following:

  • SDPO induces overfitting, with degraded performance on either new problems or out-of-distribution tasks
  • OPSD does not rely on privileged information, instead depending on the Qwen3 thinking-mode toggles
  • Self-distillation gradients point the wrong way, breaking self-distillation assumptions

Together, we believe these findings highlight the need to develop reinforcement learning algorithms that can leverage privileged information to robustly boost performance. A niche we claim that self-distillation does not fill.

What does self-distillation promise?

Wait; what made self-distillation so appealing to begin with? Let us have a peek at some results and claims made in self-distillation papers.

OPSD claims that having a model internalize ground-truth solutions (via self-distillation) allows it to “teach itself”. This contrasts with the standard reinforcement learning paradigm, which learns by trial and error (e.g., GRPO needs both successful and unsuccessful rollouts to learn).

SDPO claims to improve over GRPO performance on LiveCodeBench v6, by leveraging the “model’s ability to retrospectively identify its own mistakes in-context” and dense logit-level feedback to achieve both sample complexity and performance gains.

SDPO claims to demonstrate generalization and wall-clock speedups on hard reasoning tasks, training on science reasoning and tool use tasks.

On standard math benchmarks, OPSD claims that the use of privileged information yields consistent performance gains over GRPO, by “utilizing its own rationalization ability to grade its weaker self without access to the ground truth.”

This is why self-distillation is appealing: it promises to allow us to use the model’s own internalization of environmental feedback to improve itself, instead of relying on external supervision.

Why might self-distillation work?

To justify self-distillation, Shenfeld et al. hypothesize that self-distillation works because feeding the model with privileged information (e.g., reference solutions) allows it to approximate the optimal policy

And indeed! We show in Proposition 3.1 of our paper that if , then self-distillation is equivalent to directly performing gradient ascent on the expected reward. Under this assumption, self-distillation should maximize the same objective as GRPO, just with better sample efficiency afforded by dense logit-level feedback.

How the cookie crumbles

Well? How well does this assumption hold? How well do self-distillation gradients align with reward maximization gradients? We measure exactly this.

Cosine similarity between training gradients and the test-set reward maximization gradient on LiveCodeBench v6
Method Qwen3-8B Qwen3-14B Olmo-3-7B-Instruct
GRPO +0.121 +0.070 +0.422
SDPO −0.167 +0.013 +0.062
Cosine similarity between training gradients and the test-set reward maximization gradient on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT 25
Method Qwen3-1.7B Qwen3-4B Qwen3-8B Qwen3-14B Olmo-3-7B-Instruct
GRPO +0.018 +0.060 +0.118 +0.166 +0.026
OPSD −0.205 −0.132 −0.160 −0.075 +0.057

This seems to indicate that by and large1, self-distillation gradients are orthogonal or even anti-aligned with the reward maximization gradient. By a Taylor series argument, with small enough steps, following the self-distillation gradient will not improve the expected reward, and may even hurt it.

Wait, so how do you explain the previously reported performance gains?

Overfitting abounds

Note the following excerpt from page 8 of the SDPO paper:

We consider a setting with public and private unit tests, common for code contests and coding platforms like LeetCode, where the public tests are used for evaluation during training and the private tests are used for validation.

In other words, SDPO evaluates on the same LiveCodeBench v6 problems it trains on, doing train-test splitting only across unit tests. Doing proper train-test splitting across problems yields the following curves:

We see that although SDPO learns faster than GRPO on the training set (on both seen and unseen unit tests), it overfits to the training problems, and performs worse than GRPO on unseen problems. Moreover, training for longer than the ~80 steps that SDPO uses (marked in red) shows that GRPO beats even SDPO on the training problems given enough time.

How about SDPO’s reported gains on science reasoning and tool use tasks?

In-domain accuracy of Qwen3-8B after 200 steps, by training domain
Biology Chemistry Material Physics Tool use Avg
SDPO 52.5 77.7 73.5 73.1 53.5 66.1
GRPO 51.0 68.9 76.2 72.4 66.3 67.0
OOD change (mean accuracy change over all non-training domains) of Qwen3-8B after 200 steps, by training domain
Biology Chemistry Material Physics Tool use Avg
SDPO −12.8 −16.6 −7.1 −12.5 +0.9 −9.6
GRPO +1.2 +1.6 +1.2 +0.9 −2.1 +0.6

We find that although SDPO and GRPO perform similarly on the training domains, SDPO degrades performance on out-of-distribution domains, consistent with the overfitting hypothesis.

Unprivileged information

Recall that OPSD claims that it works by “exploit[ing] the ground-truth solution directly as privileged information during training, enabling the model to serve as its own teacher”. But a careful reading of OPSD reveals that the OPSD teacher differs from its student in two ways: the teacher sees the reference solution, and the teacher has Qwen3’s thinking mode turned on, while the student has it turned off. Moreover, note that they also report validation performance with thinking mode turned on.

So which one matters? We find that really, it doesn’t matter what you feed into the model; you can feed a random solution or no solution at all, and OPSD performance is largely unchanged and even improves in some cases.

Thinking-on accuracy of Qwen3-8B; denotes the reference solution for the OPSD teacher, with teacher thinking on during OPSD training
Method AIME24 AIME25 HMMT25 Avg
Base 75.6 68.6 45.0 63.1
OPSD, ref 77.2 71.6 46.4 65.0
OPSD, no 78.1 71.0 46.7 65.3
OPSD, shuffled 78.3 71.2 45.9 65.1

Note that these thinking-on gains are small to begin with. The difference becomes much clearer when we evaluate with thinking off, the same mode the student is trained in:

Average thinking-off accuracy (AIME24, AIME25, HMMT25) of Qwen3-8B; the base model scores 19.3
Ref No Shuffled
OPSD (teacher think) 33.1 44.6 33.2
OPSD (teacher no think) 19.5 20.4 19.1

Turning on teacher thinking improves thinking-off accuracy by 17.3 points on average, while swapping in the reference solution of a different problem changes it by at most 0.4 points. Without teacher thinking, OPSD barely improves over the base model at all.

Looking at the generations, we find that thinking-off students trained with a thinking teacher learn to think anyway, breaking their non-thinking mode, and this is what leads to performance improvements. OPSD’s gains come from leaking thinking-mode behavior into the non-thinking mode, which requires no privileged information at all.

Conclusion

So, does self-distillation improve reasoning? Not in the way it promises to.

Self-distillation was supposed to let a model teach itself, turning privileged information into a dense, sample-efficient learning signal. Instead, we find that its reported gains either don’t generalize, or don’t come from privileged information at all:

  • SDPO improves on the problems it trains on, at the cost of new problems and other domains
  • OPSD gains just as much or more when the reference solution is shuffled or removed; what it really transfers is thinking-mode behavior
  • Both produce gradients that largely point away from reward maximization on held-out problems

We hope that this work encourages algorithmic development of reinforcement learning methods that actually leverage privileged information to yield robust performance gains.

item.title: Good teachers don’t cheat
item.dc:creator: Jason Ken Adhinarta
item.description:
TL;DR: Policy gradient RL, self-distillation techniques like SDFT, and Pedagogical RL can all be viewed as optimizing the same objective , just with slightly different optimization procedures. The privileged information that some of these methods feed in context is simply a tool to make the optimization of easier. The punchline is that, at optimality, the teacher’s use of has to vanish: good teachers don’t cheat.

Background

As a caveat, we note that some policy gradient methods actually train with for RLVR problems. However, from RL’s Razor we know that on-policy RL methods implicitly bound KL divergence, making this a reasonable assumption.

Privileged information, and why good teachers don’t cheat

Now suppose we have privileged information (for example, is an expert demonstration of a problem ) that makes it easier to obtain high rewards. In the simplest case for some deterministic function (e.g., a lookup table over stored answers).

The KL term is what makes this work, despite being possibly vanishingly small. Suppose is an expert demonstration containing the final answer, say . Then achieves the optimal reward, but it has extremely high KL divergence from , and is therefore not feasible to distill into the student. It is difficult to distill a teacher which simply repeats the final answer into the student.

RL, self-distillation, and Pedagogical RL are all equivalent

This gives us two ways to optimize the same objective:

  • Start from . Sparse rewards, but . GRPO and the like.
  • Start from . Dense rewards, but large KL. Pedagogical RL and on-policy-distillation follow this paradigm.

Importantly, KL divergence is significantly easier to optimize than sparse rewards, since rich gradients can be derived from full per-token logits (see this).

The above motivates the following two-stage procedure:

  1. Train the teacher to optimize . At optimality, loses its dependence on .
  2. Distill the teacher into the student via KL minimization, since is not available at test time. The direction of the KL is exactly the choice between two distillation methods:
    1. Minimizing is exactly on-policy distillation.
    2. Minimizing is equivalent to maximizing , which is standard off-policy SFT, which Pedagogical RL argues is more sample-efficient than on-policy distillation.

So policy gradients, self-distillation, and Pedagogical RL can be interpreted as three different optimization procedures for the same underlying objective , differing in their use of and the direction of KL minimization.

Self-distillation woes

The problem with most on-policy distillation techniques is that the teacher is never trained to optimize , step 1 is skipped! As a result, the teacher is not guaranteed to lose its dependence on , and on-policy distillation leaks the privileged information straight into the student. This probably causes the various stability issues observed in on-policy-distillation methods, with student and teacher logits diverging irreconcilably.

This post hints at the direction of some ongoing work; more to come!
